newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerians vote on draft constitution.
newsitem.headline: Algerians vote on draft constitution.

text.p: Algerians, who have endured almost five years of civil strife, have been urged by Islamic radicals and the main opposition parties to stay home or vote "No" in Thursday's referendum on a new constitution.
The draft charter would bar Moslem fundamentalists -- whose impending victory at the polls led the authorities to scrap a general election in 1992 -- from seeking power through the political system.

More than 60,000 people have died in conflict between Islamic radicals and the army-backed authorities since the oil-producing North African state's promised transition from one-party rule to elected parliamentary government was sidetracked.
With Moslem rebels vowing to disrupt the vote, the state has thrown out a security blanket to guard more than 35,500 polling stations in a land five times the size of France.
Many voting booths are in schools which have been closed for classes and turned into mini-fortresses, ringed by soldiers, residents said.
Big city markets have been shut for the week and patrolled by thousands of paratroopers, police and paramilitary forces.
President Liamine Zeroual, a former army general, is hoping to match the 75 percent turnout reported in the election which endorsed him in office in last year.
But analysts and diplomats said that hopes for change which flowered last year withered when violence continued and people felt the hardship of economic reforms required by overseas creditors.
"A year after the presidential election, political deadlock is still total," secular opposition leader Said Saadi said on Wednesday. "Social poverty is worsening every day."
This is Algeria's sixth referendum on constitutional reforms since independence from France in 1962.
Previous turnouts have been recorded as between 78 and 99 percent -- in the days when the National Liberation Front, leader of the independence struggle, held a monopoly on power.
This time opposition parties are telling supporters that if the draft is endorsed the result will be "institutional dictatorship".
The new constitution would bar politicians from campaigning on the basis of the Moslem faith, the Arab or Berber languages, gender issues or regional differences.
In northeastern, Berber-dominated areas a general strike against the proposed constitution started on Wednesday.
The draft makes Arabic sole official language of the state -- angering those who want Berber as an alternative.
The Armed Islamic Group or GIA -- most feared of the Moslem guerrilla movements -- has warned people not to vote, threatening to "break the neck" of anyone who leaves home on referendum day.
Government ministers and their political backers crossed the country urging 16.4 million eligible voters to back the draft.
"The vote in the proposed constitution is the most important event since last year's presidential election," the official Algerian news agency declared on Wednesday night.
